claim: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) co-opts the host protein CypA to aid evasion of antiviral responses dependent on the effector protein kinase R (PKR).
source: Here, we show that hepatitis C virus (HCV) co-opts the host protein CypA to aid evasion of antiviral responses dependent on the effector protein kinase R (PKR).
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experiments showing that CypA is required for HCV to evade PKR-dependent antiviral responses.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of CypA rescues PKR from antagonism by HCV NS5A.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of CypA rescues PKR from antagonism by HCV NS5A, leading to activation of an interferon regulatory factor-1 (IRF1)-driven cell intrinsic antiviral program that inhibits viral replication.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that CypI treatment leads to PKR-dependent activation of IRF1 and antiviral gene expression.

claim: CypA inhibition leads to activation of an interferon regulatory factor-1 (IRF1)-driven cell intrinsic antiviral program that inhibits viral replication.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of CypA rescues PKR from antagonism by HCV NS5A, leading to activation of an interferon regulatory factor-1 (IRF1)-driven cell intrinsic antiviral program that inhibits viral replication.
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments showing that CypI treatment induces IRF1-dependent antiviral gene expression and that IRF1 knockout reduces CypI potency.

claim: CypA is a cofactor for a variety of established and emerging viruses, including Flaviviridae such as hepatitis C virus (HCV) and dengue virus, as well as Coronaviridae such as SARS coronavirus.
source: Cyclophilin A (CypA) is a cofactor for a variety of established and emerging viruses, including Flaviviridae such as hepatitis C virus (HCV) (Yang et al., 2008) and dengue virus (Qing et al., 2009), as well as Coronaviridae such as SARS coronavirus (Pfefferle et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies demonstrating CypA's role in various viral infections.

claim: CypA has peptidyl prolyl isomerase activity, which is thought to induce conformational changes in bound target proteins.
source: Like other Cyps, CypA has peptidyl prolyl isomerase activity, which is thought to induce conformational changes in bound target proteins (Wang and Heitman, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on CypA enzymatic activity.

claim: Recruitment of CypA affects protein complex formation.
source: Importantly, recruitment of CypA also affects protein complex formation (Liu et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: CypA binds to the HIV-1 viral capsid to regulate interactions with downstream cofactors and protect the capsid and encapsidated viral genome from cellular innate immune sensors.
source: The role of CypA as a viral cofactor is best understood for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV-1), where CypA binds to the viral capsid (Luban et al., 1993; Thali et al., 1994) to regulate interactions with downstream cofactors and protect the capsid and encapsidated viral genome from cellular innate immune sensors (Rasaiyaah et al., 2013; Schaller et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies on HIV-1 and CypA.

claim: Cyps have been implicated in the regulation of viral innate immune evasion and innate immune signalling.
source: Cyps have been implicated in the regulation of viral innate immune evasion (Rasaiyaah et al., 2013) and innate immune signalling (Sun et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2017; Obata et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Clinical trials demonstrated that pharmacological inhibition of CypA suppressed HCV replication and led to elevated type one interferon (IFN) in patients.
source: In the case of HCV, clinical trials demonstrated that pharmacological inhibition of CypA suppressed HCV replication and led to elevated type one interferon (IFN) in patients (Hopkins et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to clinical trial data.

claim: Both CypA binding and resistance to cyclophilin inhibitors (CypI) map to the HCV NS5A protein.
source: Both CypA binding and resistance to cyclophilin inhibitors (CypI) map to the HCV NS5A protein (Hanoulle et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2010), which has essential roles in HCV replication and assembly (Ross-Thriepland and Harris, 2015) and crucially also contributes to immune evasion by several key mechanisms.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: HCV NS5A has essential roles in HCV replication and assembly and contributes to immune evasion by several key mechanisms.
source: Both CypA binding and resistance to cyclophilin inhibitors (CypI) map to the HCV NS5A protein (Hanoulle et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2010), which has essential roles in HCV replication and assembly (Ross-Thriepland and Harris, 2015) and crucially also contributes to immune evasion by several key mechanisms.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous review.

claim: NS5A is necessary for formation of the membranous replication organelle (RO) that cloaks viral RNA replication from cytosolic pattern recognition receptors, preventing innate immune activation.
source: For example, NS5A is necessary for formation of the membranous replication organelle (RO) (Romero-Brey et al., 2012) that cloaks viral RNA replication from cytosolic pattern recognition receptors (Neufeldt et al., 2016), preventing innate immune activation.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CypA plays a role in the formation of the HCV replication organelle (RO).
source: Notably, CypA plays a role in the formation of the RO (Madan et al., 2014; Chatterji et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NS5A inhibits activation of the key antiviral effector protein kinase R (PKR).
source: NS5A also inhibits activation of the key antiviral effector protein kinase R (PKR) (Gale et al., 1997) and subsequent PKR-dependent activation of interferon regulatory factor-1 (IRF1)-driven antiviral responses (Pflugheber et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NS5A inhibits PKR-dependent activation of interferon regulatory factor-1 (IRF1)-driven antiviral responses.
source: NS5A also inhibits activation of the key antiviral effector protein kinase R (PKR) (Gale et al., 1997) and subsequent PKR-dependent activation of interferon regulatory factor-1 (IRF1)-driven antiviral responses (Pflugheber et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Huh7.5 cells were selected for enhanced ability to support HCV replication and spread.
source: Huh7.5 cells were selected for enhanced ability to support HCV replication (Blight et al., 2002) and spread (Koutsoudakis et al., 2007), and also have defective innate immunity (Sumpter et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Huh7.5 cells have defective innate immunity.
source: Huh7.5 cells were selected for enhanced ability to support HCV replication (Blight et al., 2002) and spread (Koutsoudakis et al., 2007), and also have defective innate immunity (Sumpter et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Silencing of CypB expression inhibited HCV replication by ~100 fold in both Huh7 and Huh7.5 cell lines.
source: Silencing of CypB expression inhibited HCV replication by ~100 fold in both cell lines (Figure 1C), consistent with its previously described role in viral RNA replication (Watashi et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and consistent with previous studies.

claim: Silencing of CypA abrogated HCV replication in Huh7 cells but had minimal effect in Huh7.5 cells.
source: Intriguingly, silencing of CypA abrogated HCV replication in Huh7 cells but had minimal effect in Huh7.5 cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: CsA abrogated HCV replication in Huh7 cells, but only partially inhibited replication in Huh7.5 cells.
source: CsA abrogated HCV replication in Huh7 cells, but only partially inhibited replication in Huh7.5 cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: CsA inhibited HCV replication in Huh7.5 cells silenced for CypA expression with similar antiviral potency regardless of CypA expression.
source: CsA also inhibited HCV replication in Huh7.5 cells silenced for CypA expression (Figure 1E), with similar antiviral potency regardless of CypA expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The observed inhibition of HCV replication by CsA in Huh7.5 cells may result from inhibition of CypB, which is also a CsA target.
source: This suggests that the observed inhibition in Huh7.5 cells may result from inhibition of CypB, which is also a CsA target (Davis et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and supported by citation showing CsA targets CypB.

claim: Both CypA and CypB have roles in HCV replication, with differential cofactor requirements between Huh7 and more permissive Huh7.5 cells.
source: This observation explains the controversy of whether CypA or CypB are HCV cofactors, by demonstrating that both have roles, and suggests differential cofactor requirements between Huh7 and more permissive Huh7.5 cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing differential effects of CypA and CypB silencing in the two cell lines.

claim: Silencing of CypA expression completely inhibited HCVcc infection in Huh7 cells, but only weakly inhibited infection in Huh7.5 cells.
source: Silencing of CypA expression, or addition of CsA, completely inhibited HCVcc infection in Huh7 cells, but only weakly inhibited infection in Huh7.5 cells (Figure 1F–G), which may reflect a role for CypA in HCV assembly (Nag et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F-G.

claim: Addition of CsA completely inhibited HCVcc infection in Huh7 cells, but only weakly inhibited infection in Huh7.5 cells.
source: Silencing of CypA expression, or addition of CsA, completely inhibited HCVcc infection in Huh7 cells, but only weakly inhibited infection in Huh7.5 cells (Figure 1F–G), which may reflect a role for CypA in HCV assembly (Nag et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F-G.

claim: The weak inhibition of HCVcc infection by CypA silencing in Huh7.5 cells may reflect a role for CypA in HCV assembly.
source: Silencing of CypA expression, or addition of CsA, completely inhibited HCVcc infection in Huh7 cells, but only weakly inhibited infection in Huh7.5 cells (Figure 1F–G), which may reflect a role for CypA in HCV assembly (Nag et al., 2012).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to previous work on CypA's role in HCV assembly.

claim: HCV DEYN replicated at wild type levels in Huh7.5 cells, but exhibited a 5-fold replication defect in innate immune competent Huh7 cells.
source: HCV DEYN replicated at wild type levels in Huh7.5 cells, but exhibited a 5-fold replication defect in innate immune competent Huh7 cells (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The replication defect of HCV DEYN in Huh7 cells was partially rescued by addition of CsA.
source: The replication defect in Huh7 cells was partially rescued by addition of CsA (Figure 1I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: CypA is crucial for HCV replication in innate sensing competent Huh7 cells, but significantly less important for replication in more permissive Huh7.5 cells.
source: Together, these results confirm that CypA is crucial for HCV replication in innate sensing competent Huh7 cells, but significantly less important for replication in more permissive Huh7.5 cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: CsA binds to the cyclophilin active site and forms a ternary inhibitory complex with phosphatase calcineurin, which inhibits T cell proliferation leading to immunosuppression.
source: CsA binds to the cyclophilin active site and forms a ternary inhibitory complex with phosphatase calcineurin, which inhibits T cell proliferation leading to immunosuppression (Liu et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Depsin molecules do not cause immunosuppression via the calcineurin pathway.
source: Importantly, depsin molecules do not cause immunosuppression via the calcineurin pathway (Zenke et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The selected CypI molecules bound to CypA with similar nanomolar affinities.
source: Using a fluorescence polarisation assay, in which fluorescent CsA is competed from purified recombinant CypA with unlabelled CypI (Warne et al., 2016), we first confirmed that the selected molecules bound to CypA with similar nanomolar affinities (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: CsA-Prtc1 treatment led to degradation of CypA in Huh7 and Huh7.5 cells.
source: CsA-Prtc1 treatment led to degradation of CypA in Huh7 and Huh7.5 cells (Figure 2C) within a matter of hours (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), with complete loss of detectable CypA protein expression occurring within 24 hr at concentrations as low as 100 nM.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-E and supplementary figures.

claim: CsA-Prtc1-mediated CypA degradation was proteasome-dependent.
source: Degradation was proteasome-dependent (Figure 2F) with selectivity for CypA (Figure 2G–H), with minimal impact on CypB or CypD protein expression after 24 hr in Huh7 cells, although CypB degradation was observed after 48 hr incubation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F-H and supplementary figures.

claim: CsA-Prtc1 has selectivity for CypA, with minimal impact on CypB or CypD protein expression after 24 hr in Huh7 cells.
source: Degradation was proteasome-dependent (Figure 2F) with selectivity for CypA (Figure 2G–H), with minimal impact on CypB or CypD protein expression after 24 hr in Huh7 cells, although CypB degradation was observed after 48 hr incubation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G-H and supplementary figures.

claim: CsA treatment protected CypA from CsA-Prtc1-mediated degradation.
source: Moreover, CsA treatment protected CypA from CsA-Prtc1-mediated degradation (Figure 2I), illustrating CypA recruitment of CsA within cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Three novel and structurally distinct CypI abrogated HCV replication in Huh7 cells, but only partially inhibited replication in Huh7.5 cells at the tested dose.
source: Like CsA, our three novel and structurally distinct CypI abrogated HCV replication (Figure 3A) and HCVcc infection (Figure 3B) in Huh7 cells, but only partially inhibited replication and infection in Huh7.5 cells at the tested dose (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: CsA-Prtc1 completely inhibited HCVcc infection in both Huh7 and Huh7.5 cell lines at the single dose tested.
source: The CsA-Prtc1 was extremely potent and completely inhibited HCVcc infection in both cell lines at the single dose tested (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The CypI were 5- to 10-fold more potent against HCV replication in Huh7 cells compared to Huh7.5 cells.
source: However, dose-response analyses showed that the CypI were similarly 5- to 10-fold more potent against HCV replication in Huh7 cells compared to Huh7.5 cells (Figure 3C), with low nanomolar IC50 in Huh7 cells (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Table 1.

claim: The selected CypI were more potent against HCVcc infection of Huh7 cells compared to Huh7.5 cells.
source: The selected CypI were similarly more potent against HCVcc infection of Huh7 cells compared to Huh7.5 cells (Figure 3D, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Table 1.

claim: CypI treatment dose-dependently enhanced DEYN replication in Huh7 cells while replication of the NS5A DEYN mutant was resistant to CypI treatment in Huh7.5 cells.
source: Concordantly, while replication of the NS5A DEYN mutant was resistant to CypI treatment in Huh7.5 cells, CypI treatment dose-dependently enhanced DEYN replication in Huh7 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), again illustrating the differential requirements for CypA in the two cell lines during HCV replication.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: CsA treatment induced expression of IFN-β in Huh7 cells but not in more permissive Huh7.5 cells.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, we observed induction of IFN-β expression in Huh7 cells but not in more permissive Huh7.5 cells (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: CsA-like molecules and structurally unrelated depsins, but not CsA-Prtc1, were capable of inducing IFN-β expression in HCV-replicating Huh7 cells.
source: Intriguingly, CsA-like molecules and structurally unrelated depsins, but not CsA-Prtc1 (which degrades CypA rather than simply binding CypA and affecting complex formation), were capable of inducing IFN-β expression in HCV-replicating Huh7 cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Activation of IFN-β expression by CypI requires the presence of CypA.
source: One possibility is that activation of IFN-β expression requires the presence of CypA, which is consistent with previous studies suggesting CypA is a necessary co-factor for innate immune sensors, including RIG-I (Liu et al., 2017) and PKR (Daito et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that CsA-Prtc1 (which degrades CypA) does not induce IFN-β, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ruxolitinib treatment rescued HCV replication from IFN-β inhibition but did not affect the potency of CsA or other CypI against HCV replication in Huh7 cells.
source: Although pharmacological inhibition of the Jak/STAT pathway by ruxolitinib treatment rescued HCV replication from inhibition by IFN-β (Figure 4D), ruxolitinib treatment had no effect on viral replication in the absence of exogenous IFN-β. Furthermore, ruxolitinib did not affect the potency of CsA (Figure 4E) or other CypI (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) against HCV replication in Huh7 cells, suggesting that the antiviral effect is independent of IFN signalling.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D-E and supplementary figures.

claim: The antiviral effect of CypI is independent of IFN signalling.
source: Although pharmacological inhibition of the Jak/STAT pathway by ruxolitinib treatment rescued HCV replication from inhibition by IFN-β (Figure 4D), ruxolitinib treatment had no effect on viral replication in the absence of exogenous IFN-β. Furthermore, ruxolitinib did not affect the potency of CsA (Figure 4E) or other CypI (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) against HCV replication in Huh7 cells, suggesting that the antiviral effect is independent of IFN signalling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that blocking IFN signaling does not affect CypI potency.

claim: Anti-IFNAR treatment did not affect the potency of CsA against HCV but effectively rescued HCV replication from inhibition by IFN-β.
source: The notion that IFN was not required for maximal CypI activity was also supported by an experiment using anti-human interferon alpha/beta receptor chain two antibody (IFNAR) to inhibit IFN activity through receptor blockade. Anti-IFNAR treatment did not affect the potency of CsA against HCV but effectively rescued HCV replication from inhibition by IFN-β in a control experiment. (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A-B.

claim: CypI induces direct expression of antiviral genes with inhibitory activity against HCV, including viperin (RSAD2), in Huh7 but not Huh7.5 cells.
source: The lack of a requirement for IFN in the effect of CypI is likely explained by direct induction of antiviral genes with inhibitory activity against HCV, here exemplified by viperin (RSAD2) (Helbig et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2012), in Huh7 but not Huh7.5 cells (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F and supplementary figures, and citations to previous work on viperin's anti-HCV activity.

claim: CypI induces IFN-independent, cell-intrinsic antiviral immunity in these experiments.
source: Thus, we propose that in these experiments, CypI induces IFN-independent, cell-intrinsic antiviral immunity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that CypI activity is independent of IFN signaling but induces antiviral gene expression.

claim: In vivo, IFN induction would be expected to influence HCV replication and adaptive immune responses and thus the antiviral activity of CypI in patients.
source: However, in vivo, IFN induction would be expected to influence HCV replication and adaptive immune responses and thus the antiviral activity of CypI in patients.
evidence: This is speculation about the in vivo effects based on the in vitro findings.

claim: Silencing of CypA expression by RNAi or treatment with a CsA analogue (cyclosporine D) inhibited formation of the double membrane vesicles (DMVs) that comprise the HCV RO.
source: CypA has previously been implicated in formation of the HCV RO. Silencing of CypA expression by RNAi (Chatterji et al., 2015) or treatment with a CsA analogue (cyclosporine D) (Madan et al., 2014) inhibited formation of the double membrane vesicles (DMVs) that comprise the HCV RO, thus inhibiting HCV replication.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CypI treatment did not affect expression of NS5A.
source: CypI treatment did not affect expression of NS5A as measured by immunofluorescence (Figure 5A) and western blot (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Treatment with CsA, depsin or CsA-Prtc1 caused a significant reduction in the number and size of DMVs observed by transmission electron microscopy (TEM) in transfected cells.
source: However, treatment with CsA, depsin or CsA-Prtc1 caused a significant reduction in the number and size of DMVs observed by transmission electron microscopy (TEM) in transfected cells (Figure 5C–E), suggesting incomplete and impaired formation of the RO.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-E.

claim: Stable expression of RIG-I or Mda5 (or both) had little, if any, effect on HCV replication at 48 hr.
source: However, stable expression of RIG-I or Mda5 (or both) had little, if any, effect on HCV replication at 48 hr (Figure 6A) and, more importantly, did not affect the antiviral potency of the CypI in Huh7.5 cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: Stable expression of RIG-I or Mda5 (or both) did not affect the antiviral potency of the CypI in Huh7.5 cells.
source: However, stable expression of RIG-I or Mda5 (or both) had little, if any, effect on HCV replication at 48 hr (Figure 6A) and, more importantly, did not affect the antiviral potency of the CypI in Huh7.5 cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: Transient transfection of RIG-I into Huh7.5 cells did not affect HCV replication or CypI potency.
source: Similarly, transient transfection of RIG-I into Huh7.5 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) did not affect HCV replication (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), consistent with previous findings (Binder et al., 2007), or CypI potency (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and citation to previous work.

claim: The loss of MAVS did not affect HCV replication compared to control cells.
source: The loss of MAVS did not affect HCV replication evaluated compared to control cells (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Exogenous expression of WT or HCV protease-resistant MAVS mutant C508R into MAVS KO Huh7 cells decreased viral replication.
source: However, exogenous expression of WT or HCV protease-resistant MAVS mutant C508R (Li et al., 2005) into MAVS KO Huh7 cells decreased viral replication (Figure 6E), likely due to induction of interferon responses (Bender et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E and citations to previous work.

claim: The antiviral potency of CypI was unaffected by the absence of MAVS.
source: Crucially, the antiviral potency of CypI was unaffected by the absence of MAVS (Figure 6F), and transfection of the C508R protease-resistant MAVS into MAVS KO Huh7 cells also had no effect on CypI activity (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: CypI still induced expression of IFN-β mRNA in HCV-replicating MAVS KO Huh7 cells.
source: Furthermore, CypI still induced expression of IFN-β mRNA in HCV-replicating MAVS KO Huh7 cells (Figure 6G), indicating that CypI induction of IFN-β expression is not dependant on the RLR/MAVS pathway.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: CypI induction of IFN-β expression is not dependent on the RLR/MAVS pathway.
source: Furthermore, CypI still induced expression of IFN-β mRNA in HCV-replicating MAVS KO Huh7 cells (Figure 6G), indicating that CypI induction of IFN-β expression is not dependant on the RLR/MAVS pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing IFN-β induction in MAVS KO cells.

claim: Treatment with daclatasvir inhibits HCV replication without inducing IFN-β expression.
source: It is worth noting that treatment with daclatasvir, an inhibitor that similarly blocks formation of the HCV RO (Berger et al., 2014) and targets domain I of NS5A (Gao et al., 2010), inhibits HCV replication without inducing IFN-β expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A-B and citations to previous work.

claim: Sensing of viral RNA in the presence of CypI is likely not the result of simply 'uncloaking' by disruption of the RO but rather through a more complex CypA-dependent mechanism.
source: Therefore, sensing of viral RNA in the presence of CypI is likely not the result of simply 'uncloaking' by disruption of the RO but rather through a more complex CypA-dependent mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that daclatasvir (which also disrupts the RO) does not induce IFN-β.

claim: NS5A domain II (where CypA binds) is dispensable for RO formation but is required to suppress IFN and control PKR.
source: Notably, NS5A domain II (where CypA binds) is dispensable for RO formation (Romero-Brey et al., 2015) but is required to suppress IFN (Hiet et al., 2015) and control PKR (Gale et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PKR was more abundant in Huh7 cells than in Huh7.5 cells.
source: Importantly, PKR was more abundant in Huh7 cells, and, strikingly PKR T446 autophosphorylation (a marker of PKR activation) was observed in Huh7 but decreased in Huh7.5 cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: PKR T446 autophosphorylation (a marker of PKR activation) was observed in Huh7 but decreased in Huh7.5 cells.
source: Importantly, PKR was more abundant in Huh7 cells, and, strikingly PKR T446 autophosphorylation (a marker of PKR activation) was observed in Huh7 but decreased in Huh7.5 cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The antiviral potency of the CypI against HCV replication and HCVcc infection was markedly decreased in PKR KO cells.
source: The antiviral potency of the CypI against HCV replication and HCVcc infection was markedly decreased (Figure 7D–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D-E.

claim: CsA treatment failed to induce IFN-β mRNA expression in HCV-replicating PKR KO Huh7 cells.
source: Importantly, CsA treatment failed to induce IFN-β mRNA expression in HCV-replicating PKR KO Huh7 cells (Figure 7F), further supporting the model in which induction of IFN, and anti-HCV restriction factors, is mediated through PKR in the presence of CypI.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: C16 decreased CsA potency in Huh7 cells, but not in Huh7 PKR KO cells.
source: C16 decreased CsA potency in Huh7 cells, but not in Huh7 PKR KO cells (Figure 7G), and only minimally affected CsA potency against HCV in Huh7.5 cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7G and supplementary figures.

claim: The absence of PKR did not affect the inhibitory activity of telaprevir or daclatasvir against HCV.
source: Unlike Cyp inhibition (Figure 7D–E), the absence of PKR did not affect the inhibitory activity of telaprevir or daclatasvir (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: PKR has a specific role in the enhanced antiviral activity of CypI in Huh7 cells.
source: Collectively, these data are consistent with a specific role for PKR in the enhanced antiviral activity of CypI in Huh7 cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that PKR knockout specifically affects CypI potency but not other antivirals.

claim: CypI inhibited PKR autophosphorylation in HCV-replicating cells.
source: Consistently, we observed that our CypI inhibited PKR autophosphorylation in HCV-replicating cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A) while only minimally affecting PKR expression based on densitometry analysis (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: CsA predominantly induced expression of IRF1 target genes, and not canonical NF-κB targets.
source: Interestingly, CsA predominantly induced expression of IRF1 target genes, and not canonical NF-κB targets (Yamane et al., 2019; Figure 4F), and this induction was PKR-dependent in both HCV-replicating (Figure 8A) and HCVcc-infected cells (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 8A-B, and citation to previous work.

claim: Induction of IRF1 target genes by CsA was PKR-dependent in both HCV-replicating and HCVcc-infected cells.
source: Interestingly, CsA predominantly induced expression of IRF1 target genes, and not canonical NF-κB targets (Yamane et al., 2019; Figure 4F), and this induction was PKR-dependent in both HCV-replicating (Figure 8A) and HCVcc-infected cells (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A-B.

claim: Restriction of HCV replication by CypI depends on the PKR-mediated induction of antiviral gene expression, including IRF1 targets.
source: Thus, restriction of HCV replication by CypI depends on the PKR-mediated induction of antiviral gene expression, including IRF1 targets.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing PKR-dependent induction of IRF1 target genes.

claim: IRF1 and several IRF1 target genes have been shown to negatively regulate HCV replication.
source: Notably, IRF1 and several IRF1 target genes have been shown to negatively regulate HCV replication (Kanazawa et al., 2004; Yamane et al., 2019), such as RSAD2 (viperin) (Helbig et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CsA-Prtc1 treatment did not induce expression of IRF1 target genes.
source: Unlike CsA, CsA-Prtc1 treatment did not induce expression of IRF1 target genes (Figure 8—figure supplement 2), consistent with our earlier findings evaluating IFN-β expression (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: CsA treatment did not induce expression of IRF1 target genes in the Huh7.5 cells.
source: Importantly, CsA treatment did not induce expression of these genes in the Huh7.5 cells, which we propose are defective for PKR function (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The antiviral potency of the CypI against HCV replication was markedly decreased in the IRF1 KO cells.
source: Strikingly, the antiviral potency of the CypI against HCV replication was markedly decreased in the IRF1 KO cells (Figure 8D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The effect of IRF1 KO closely matched the phenotype observed in the PKR KO cells.
source: Importantly, the effect of IRF1 KO closely matched the phenotype we observed in the PKR KO cells (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is an observation comparing the experimental results from IRF1 KO and PKR KO cells.

claim: PKR signalling through IRF1 determines the potency of CypI against HCV.
source: Collectively, these findings demonstrate that PKR signalling through IRF1 determines the potency of CypI against HCV.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that both PKR and IRF1 are required for maximal CypI potency.

claim: CypA is a critical host factor for many viruses.
source: CypA is a critical host factor for many viruses, although the mechanisms underlying its remarkably broad usage as a viral host factor remain unclear.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the field.

claim: CypA is crucial for HCV evasion of PKR-dependent, but not RLR/MAVS-dependent, antiviral responses.
source: We found that CypA is crucial for HCV evasion of PKR-dependent, but not RLR/MAVS-dependent, antiviral responses.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings supported by the experimental data.

claim: A deficiency in PKR-dependent responses, as well as defective RIG-I, may contribute to Huh7.5 cell permissivity for HCV replication.
source: Furthermore, our results suggest that a deficiency in PKR-dependent responses, as well as defective RIG-I (Sumpter et al., 2005), may contribute to Huh7.5 cell permissivity for HCV replication, which is consistent with previous observations showing that RIG-I does not play a role (Binder et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: CypB forms a complex with NS5A and NS5B to directly regulate HCV RNA replication.
source: We propose a model where CypB forms a complex with NS5A and NS5B to directly regulate HCV RNA replication, while CypA forms a complex with NS5A and PKR, leading to inhibition of PKR-dependent antiviral responses (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings and illustrated in Figure 9.

claim: CypA forms a complex with NS5A and PKR, leading to inhibition of PKR-dependent antiviral responses.
source: We propose a model where CypB forms a complex with NS5A and NS5B to directly regulate HCV RNA replication, while CypA forms a complex with NS5A and PKR, leading to inhibition of PKR-dependent antiviral responses (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings and illustrated in Figure 9.

claim: CypI directly inhibit HCV replication in both Huh7 and Huh7.5 cells by targeting CypB.
source: CypI, which target both CypA and CypB (Davis et al., 2010), directly inhibit HCV replication in both Huh7 and Huh7.5 cells by targeting CypB, and they disrupt the CypA-NS5A interaction, thus rendering them more efficacious in Huh7 cells because there they relieve NS5A inhibition of PKR and restore PKR-dependent antiviral responses.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings and supported by citation.

claim: CypI disrupt the CypA-NS5A interaction, thus rendering them more efficacious in Huh7 cells because there they relieve NS5A inhibition of PKR and restore PKR-dependent antiviral responses.
source: CypI, which target both CypA and CypB (Davis et al., 2010), directly inhibit HCV replication in both Huh7 and Huh7.5 cells by targeting CypB, and they disrupt the CypA-NS5A interaction, thus rendering them more efficacious in Huh7 cells because there they relieve NS5A inhibition of PKR and restore PKR-dependent antiviral responses.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: A differential requirement for CypA in Huh7-Lunet and Huh7.5 cells has been observed for replication of genotype 1b (Con1) and genotype 2a (JFH-1) replicons.
source: Notably, a differential requirement for CypA in Huh7-Lunet and Huh7.5 cells has also been observed for replication of genotype 1b (Con1) and genotype 2a (JFH-1) replicons (Kaul et al., 2009), suggesting that these mechanisms are consistent across HCV genotypes.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: CypA has been proposed to have a role in HCV assembly.
source: CypA has been proposed to have a role in HCV assembly (Nag et al., 2012; Anderson et al., 2011), which is likely reflected by our observation that CypA depletion in Huh7.5 cells decreased HCVcc infection (Figure 1F), but not replication of the HCV replicon (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work and consistent with the experimental observations.

claim: IRF1 exerted the most potent inhibition out of 380 ISGs screened against four positive-sense RNA viruses (including HCV, Flaviviridae and Togaviridae).
source: Furthermore, IRF1 exerted the most potent inhibition out of 380 ISGs screened against four positive-sense RNA viruses (including HCV, Flaviviridae and Togaviridae) (Schoggins et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The antiviral activity of IRF1 was independent of canonical Jak-STAT IFN signalling.
source: Consistent with our observations (Figure 7B–C), the antiviral activity of IRF1 was independent of canonical Jak-STAT IFN signalling (Schoggins et al., 2011), suggesting that IRF1 controls a unique IFN-independent antiviral program that is key for antiviral defense in hepatocytes (Yamane et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies and consistent with the experimental data.

claim: IRF1 controls a unique IFN-independent antiviral program that is key for antiviral defense in hepatocytes.
source: Consistent with our observations (Figure 7B–C), the antiviral activity of IRF1 was independent of canonical Jak-STAT IFN signalling (Schoggins et al., 2011), suggesting that IRF1 controls a unique IFN-independent antiviral program that is key for antiviral defense in hepatocytes (Yamane et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: HCV efficiently controls NF-κB and MAVS, but appears to be more sensitive to IRF1 restriction.
source: HCV efficiently controls NF-κB (Kumthip et al., 2012; Park et al., 2012) and MAVS (Li et al., 2005), but appears to be more sensitive to IRF1 restriction (Yamane et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The ability of HCV to inhibit PKR and evade downstream IRF1 responses depends critically on the CypA-NS5A interaction.
source: We propose that the ability of HCV to inhibit PKR and evade downstream IRF1 responses depends critically on the CypA-NS5A interaction, and that disruption of this interaction by CypI leads to activation of PKR and engages IRF1-dependent antiviral responses.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: Disruption of the CypA-NS5A interaction by CypI leads to activation of PKR and engages IRF1-dependent antiviral responses.
source: We propose that the ability of HCV to inhibit PKR and evade downstream IRF1 responses depends critically on the CypA-NS5A interaction, and that disruption of this interaction by CypI leads to activation of PKR and engages IRF1-dependent antiviral responses.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: CypA has been proposed as a regulator of PKR activity in the context of eIF2α phosphorylation.
source: CypA has been proposed as a regulator of PKR activity in the context of eIF2α phosphorylation (Daito et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: CypA is required for regulation of PKR in a broader context, including activation of IRF1.
source: Our data suggest that CypA is required for regulation of PKR in a broader context, including activation of IRF1, since targeting CypA for proteolytic degradation by PROTAC (e.g. CsA-Prtc1) blocked the activation of IFN-β or IRF1 target gene expression that we observed with CsA (Figure 4C, Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that CsA-Prtc1 does not induce IFN-β or IRF1 target gene expression.

claim: CypA-NS5A-PKR complex formation likely regulates PKR activation in HCV-replicating cells.
source: Given that CypA regulates protein complexes and that CypA, NS5A and PKR have all been shown to interact (Hanoulle et al., 2009; Daito et al., 2014; Gale et al., 1998), CypA-NS5A-PKR complex formation likely regulates PKR activation in HCV-replicating cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and supported by citations to previous work showing interactions between these proteins.

claim: Perturbation of the CypA-NS5A-PKR complex by CypI disrupts NS5A inhibition of PKR, but not PKR activation of IRF1.
source: Our data suggest that perturbation of the complex by CypI disrupts NS5A inhibition of PKR, but not PKR activation of IRF1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that CypI treatment leads to PKR-dependent IRF1 activation despite inhibiting PKR autophosphorylation.

claim: The mechanisms by which PKR activates NF-κB and IRF1 appear to be independent of PKR kinase activity, at least in the case of NF-κB.
source: The regulation of PKR is not fully understood (Bou-Nader et al., 2019), and the mechanisms by which PKR activates NF-κB and IRF1 in particular are unclear, although appear to be independent of PKR kinase activity, at least in the case of NF-κB (Bonnet et al., 2000; Bonnet et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Activation of IRF1 by PKR does not require canonical PKR activation mechanisms (i.e. autophosphorylation).
source: Our data suggest that activation of IRF1 by PKR does not require canonical PKR activation mechanisms (i.e. autophosphorylation), as CypI inhibit PKR autophosphorylation in HCV-replicating cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 1) but still induce PKR-dependent activation of antiviral target genes (Figure 8A–B) regulated by IRF1 and potentially other transcription factors, suggesting distinct mechanisms of PKR activation and downstream signalling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that CypI inhibit PKR autophosphorylation but still induce PKR-dependent gene expression.

claim: CypI restore PKR-dependent antiviral responses to inhibit infection.
source: Using HCV as a model, we have discovered that CypI restore PKR-dependent antiviral responses to inhibit infection.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings supported by the experimental data.

claim: CypI represent a novel and potentially broadly acting antiviral mechanism based on inhibition of viral evasion and restoration of host intrinsic antiviral immunity.
source: This represents a novel and potentially broadly acting antiviral mechanism based on inhibition of viral evasion and restoration of host intrinsic antiviral immunity.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: Many viruses require CypA, including medically important human viruses such as Flaviviridae and Coronaviridae family members.
source: Whether other viruses exploit the CypA-PKR interaction to evade antiviral immunity remains to be determined, although many viruses do require CypA (Dawar et al., 2017), including medically important (and currently untreatable) human viruses such as Flaviviridae and Coronaviridae family members (Qing et al., 2009; de Wilde et al., 2011; Pfefferle et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Many viruses encode PKR antagonists.
source: Many viruses also encode PKR antagonists, although the roles of CypA in viral PKR antagonism (beyond our current study) have not yet been elucidated.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the field.

claim: CypA is an attractive antiviral target for a broad array of viruses, including emerging human viruses currently lacking specific antiviral therapies.
source: Overall, CypA is an attractive antiviral target for a broad array of viruses, including emerging human viruses currently lacking specific antiviral therapies.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the therapeutic implications of the findings.
